title: Power analysis by simulation
text:
Power formulas exist for simple designs such as t-tests. For the models most CBB projects need (repeated observations of the same animals, counts, binary choices), they do not. Simulation works for every model: simulate data from the planned model many times, fit the model to each dataset, and count how often the effect is detected.
This follows directly from the guiding principle model before data, and the simulation code doubles as a first draft of the analysis script and of the preregistration.

title: Power analysis by simulation
text:
Simulate first
How does power change with the number of animals, when each animal is tested in 10 trials?

library(lme4)
set.seed(14)

power_lmm <- function(n_id, n_trials = 10, b1 = 0.6, sd_id = 0.6, nsim = 200) {
  mean(replicate(nsim, {
    id <- factor(rep(1:n_id, each = n_trials))
    x  <- rep(rep(0:1, length.out = n_id), each = n_trials) # between-animal condition
    u  <- rep(rnorm(n_id, 0, sd_id), each = n_trials)
    y  <- b1 * x + u + rnorm(n_id * n_trials)
    m1 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 | id), REML = FALSE)
    m0 <- lmer(y ~ 1 + (1 | id), REML = FALSE)
    anova(m0, m1)$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2] < .05
  }))
}

n_ids <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80)
pow   <- sapply(n_ids, power_lmm)

plot(n_ids, pow, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#1b6f8a", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Number of animals", ylab = "Power")
abline(h = .8, lty = 2, col = "#c0392b")

title: Bayesian modelling with brms
text:
brms is an R package for fitting Bayesian regression models, from simple linear models to complex multilevel models. You write the same formula syntax as in lme4, e.g. y ~ x + (1 | id). brms translates the model into Stan, which estimates the posterior distribution of all parameters.
This makes brms an easy entry into Bayesian modelling for anyone who knows the models from Linear Models in R: the models stay the same, only the way of estimating them and of drawing conclusions changes.

section: Worked example: the Safe-vs-Risky box study
text:
Worked example: the Safe-vs-Risky box study
We return to the example from session 11. Chimpanzees choose into which of two boxes a grape is dropped. The Safe box clearly guarantees delivery; in the Risky box, the grape seems to get stuck. In fact, both boxes always deliver.


RQ1: Do chimps prefer the Safe box on trial 1?

RQ2: Does this preference change over trials?


The study (with the MPI EVA, Leipzig) is preregistered, but the data do not exist yet. As in session 11, we use simulated data of what we expect: 15 chimps × 4 sessions × 10 trials, with an initial Safe preference (P = .70), no average change over trials, but chimps that differ in whether they drift towards Safe or Risky. So we know the true answer.

The data

Simulation code (same as session 11)side_sequence <- function() {           # 5 x right, 5 x left; max. 2 in a row
  repeat {
    s <- sample(rep(0:1, 5))
    if (max(rle(s)$lengths) <= 2) return(s)
  }
}

sim_chimps <- function(n = 15, b0 = qlogis(0.70), b.trial = 0, b.side = 0.3,
                       sd.int = 0.8, sd.slope = 0.05) {
  ids <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:n)
  u0 <- setNames(rnorm(n, 0, sd.int), ids); u1 <- setNames(rnorm(n, 0, sd.slope), ids)
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ids, function(id)
    data.frame(subject = id, session = rep(1:4, each = 10), trial = 1:40,
               side_safe = unlist(replicate(4, side_sequence(), simplify = FALSE)))))
  d$trial_c <- d$trial - 1                       # first-trial centred (as preregistered)
  eta <- b0 + u0[d$subject] + (b.trial + u1[d$subject]) * d$trial_c + b.side * d$side_safe
  d$safe <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(eta))
  d
}

set.seed(120)
chimps <- sim_chimps()



Codeby_sess <- aggregate(safe ~ subject + session, data = chimps, FUN = mean)
avg     <- aggregate(safe ~ session, data = chimps, FUN = mean)

ggplot(by_sess, aes(session, safe)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_line(aes(group = subject), colour = col_teal, alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(data = avg, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = avg, colour = col_red, size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "Safe choices",
       subtitle = "Thin lines: individual chimps · red: average")







Step 1: the GLMM from session 11

glmm <- glmer(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 + trial_c | subject),
              family = binomial, data = chimps,

Step 2: priors
A Bayesian model needs a prior for every parameter. We use weakly informative priors on the log-odds scale: they rule out absurd values but leave the data in charge.

priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),   # P(Safe) on trial 1
            prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b"),           # trial and side effects
            prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"),          # between-chimp SDs
            prior(lkj(2),         class = "cor"))         # intercept-slope correlation

What do these priors imply before seeing any data? A prior predictive check translates them into chimp-level choice probabilities on trial 1:

Codeset.seed(1)
p_trial1 <- plogis(rnorm(1e4, 0, 1.5) + rnorm(1e4, 0, rexp(1e4, 1)))
ggplot(data.frame(p = p_trial1), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = col_teal, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) on trial 1 for a chimp, implied by the priors", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())







The priors allow anything from a strong Risky to a strong Safe preference. They put somewhat more weight on extreme preferences than on 50%; a narrower intercept prior, e.g. normal(0, 1), would flatten this.
Step 3: fit the model
The formula is exactly the one from glmer(). bernoulli is the binomial family for single 0/1 choices.

fit <- brm(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 + trial_c | subject),
           family = bernoulli, data = chimps, prior = priors,
           chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 2026)


summary(fit)

#>  Family: bernoulli 
#>   Links: mu = logit 
#> Formula: safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 + trial_c | subject) 
#>    Data: chimps (Number of observations: 600) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#> 
#> Group-Level Effects: 
#> ~subject (Number of levels: 15) 
#>                        Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)              0.63      0.33     0.06     1.34 1.00     1409
#> sd(trial_c)                0.08      0.03     0.04     0.14 1.00     1226
#> cor(Intercept,trial_c)     0.20      0.36    -0.53     0.82 1.01      791
#>                        Tail_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)              1440
#> sd(trial_c)                2046
#> cor(Intercept,trial_c)     1284
#> 
#> Population-Level Effects: 
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept     1.12      0.30     0.56     1.72 1.00     3636     3105
#> trial_c      -0.02      0.02    -0.06     0.03 1.00     1916     2096
#> side_safe     0.27      0.21    -0.13     0.67 1.00     5164     2971
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).


All Rhat values are 1.00 and the effective sample sizes (ESS) are large, so the four chains agree. The trace plots should look like “hairy caterpillars”, with no chain drifting off:

Codebayesplot::mcmc_trace(as.array(fit), pars = c("b_Intercept", "b_trial_c", "sd_subject__trial_c"),
                      facet_args = list(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Step 4: answer the research questions with the posterior
The posterior is a distribution, so we can answer the research questions on the response scale and as probabilities.

draws <- as_draws_df(fit)
# P(Safe) for an average chimp, averaged over the two sides
p1  <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept +                      0.5 * draws$b_side_safe)  # trial 1
p40 <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept + 39 * draws$b_trial_c + 0.5 * draws$b_side_safe)  # trial 40


Codepost <- rbind(data.frame(trial = "Trial 1", p = p1), data.frame(trial = "Trial 40", p = p40))
ggplot(post, aes(p, fill = trial)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_density(alpha = .6, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_teal, col_red), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(.3, 1)) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) for an average chimp", y = "Posterior density")









RQ1: On trial 1, an average chimp chooses the Safe box with probability 0.78, 95% credible interval [0.68, 0.86]. The posterior probability that chimps prefer the Safe box, i.e. that P(Safe) > .5, is > .99.

RQ2: From trial 1 to trial 40, P(Safe) changes by -0.13, 95% CrI [-0.55, 0.17]. The interval is wide: these data cannot rule out a moderate change in either direction. Whether the change is practically zero is a question for an equivalence test or a ROPE (see TAE).

The model-implied learning curve, with 95% credible band:

Codece <- conditional_effects(fit, effects = "trial_c")$trial_c
ggplot(ce, aes(trial_c + 1, estimate__)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower__, ymax = upper__), fill = col_teal, alpha = .25) +
  geom_line(colour = col_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Trial", y = "P(Safe)")







Step 5: does the model reproduce the data?
A posterior predictive check simulates new datasets from the fitted model and compares them with the observed data. Here: the proportion of Safe choices for each chimp.

Codepp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", group = "subject", ndraws = 1000) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1), labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of Safe choices") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







The observed proportions (dark lines) lie well within the simulated ones for every chimp.

  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







What stays the same, and what changes


The estimates agree. With weakly informative priors and 600 observations, the posterior means and credible intervals are very close to the glmer() estimates and confidence intervals. Bayesian modelling is not a different model, but a different way of estimating it.

The interpretation changes. A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability, given model and priors. That is how most people (mis)read a confidence interval anyway. And we can directly state things like “the probability that chimps prefer the Safe box on trial 1 is > .99”.

Uncertainty about the variance components is visible. glmer() gives only point estimates for the between-chimp SDs; brms gives full intervals. The wide interval for the SD of the intercept shows how little 15 chimps tell us about individual differences.

Complex random-effects structures become easier. With only 15 individuals, glmer() often runs into convergence warnings or singular fits. The priors keep brms stable, which helps with the maximal random-effects structures recommended for confirmatory tests.

The price: more computing time (here a few minutes instead of a second) and the need to choose and justify priors.

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
text: A hands-on course that builds on Linear Models in R. Many hypotheses in behavioural research predict the absence of an effect, yet a non-significant result is often misread as evidence for it. The course teaches two ways to test such predictions properly: frequentist equivalence tests and Bayesian alternatives.

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
text:
Topics

Why p > .05 is not evidence for “no effect”: absence of evidence vs. evidence of absence.
The smallest effect size of interest (SESOI): how to justify which effects are too small to matter.
Equivalence tests (TOST): how to test predictions of “no effect” with classical significance tests, based on a justified SESOI (R package TOSTER).
Bayes factors: quantifying the evidence for the null relative to the alternative (R package BayesFactor).
Bayesian estimation with a region of practical equivalence (ROPE): deciding on the basis of the posterior distribution (R packages brms and bayestestR).
Comparing the approaches: when they agree, when they differ, and the role of priors.

Outcome: each participant plans how to test a “no effect” prediction in their own project, including a sample-size justification.

Key terms: p-value, SESOI (smallest effect size of interest), Equivalence test (TOST), Bayes factor, ROPE (region of practical equivalence), Prior, posterior

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
section: Simulate first: three answers to the same data
text:
Simulate first: three answers to the same data
There is no difference between the two groups in these data. The classic t-test is non-significant, but that alone says nothing about whether the effect is absent.

set.seed(13)
n <- 100
a <- rnorm(n); b <- rnorm(n)                 # true difference = 0
sesoi <- 0.4                                 # smallest effect of interest (in SD units)

# 1. Classic t-test: non-significant, but not evidence for "no effect"
t.test(a, b, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value

#> [1] 0.5200304

# 2. Equivalence test (TOST): is the difference within [-SESOI, +SESOI]?
p_lower <- t.test(a, b, mu = -sesoi, alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
p_upper <- t.test(a, b, mu =  sesoi, alternative = "less",    var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
max(p_lower, p_upper)                        # < .05 -> effect is statistically equivalent to zero

#> [1] 0.01766867

# 3. Bayes factor for H0 over H1 (BIC approximation; Wagenmakers, 2007)
d  <- data.frame(y = c(a, b), group = rep(c("a", "b"), each = n))
m0 <- lm(y ~ 1, data = d)
m1 <- lm(y ~ group, data = d)
exp((BIC(m1) - BIC(m0)) / 2)                 # BF01 > 1 favours "no difference"

#> [1] 11.46872


In the course, the BIC approximation is replaced by Bayes factors with explicit priors (BayesFactor) and by posterior estimation with a ROPE (brms, bayestestR).

title: Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science
text: A hands-on course that teaches tools still rarely used in behavioural research. It draws on Daniël Lakens’ open teaching materials (e.g., Improving Your Statistical Inferences) and the R package rpact.

title: Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science
text:
Topics


Preregistration and registered reports, including for observational field data and secondary analyses.

Sequential analyses: group-sequential designs with planned interim analyses and alpha spending, so data collection can stop early for efficacy without inflating the type I error.

Optional stopping and stopping for futility: why peeking at p-values inflates error rates (shown by simulation), and how to stop correctly, including when an effect is unlikely to emerge.


Why this matters at DPZ: sequential designs and stopping for futility reduce the expected number of animals per study. This directly supports the Reduction principle of the 3Rs and strengthens the justification in animal-ethics applications.

Outcome: each participant drafts a preregistration with a sample-size or sequential plan for their own project.

title: Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science
section: Simulate first: why peeking is a problem
text:
Simulate first: why peeking is a problem
There is no effect in these simulations. A researcher tests after every 10 observations per group and stops as soon as p < .05. How often do they find a “significant” result?

set.seed(12)
looks <- seq(10, 100, by = 10)
nsim  <- 2000

first_sig <- replicate(nsim, {
  a <- rnorm(max(looks)); b <- rnorm(max(looks))       # H0 is true
  p <- sapply(looks, function(n) t.test(a[1:n], b[1:n])$p.value)
  which(p < .05)[1]                                    # first look with p < .05 (NA if none)
})

alpha_by_look <- sapply(seq_along(looks), function(k) mean(!is.na(first_sig) & first_sig <= k))

plot(looks, alpha_by_look, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#c0392b", ylim = c(0, .25),
     xlab = "Maximum n per group (one look every 10)", ylab = "Type I error rate")
abline(h = .05, lty = 2, col = "#1b6f8a")







With ten looks, the false-positive rate is far above the nominal 5 %. Group-sequential designs (e.g., with rpact) fix this by spending the alpha across the planned looks.

title: Exercises · Session 11
text:
The data
Mothers’ behaviour towards their infants changes as the infants grow up. In this practical, you analyse how often wild Guinea baboon infants receive approaches from their mothers, using real field data from the DPZ field station Simenti (Senegal):

Dal Pesco, F., et al. (2026). Maternal style does not predict infant growth and survival in wild Guinea baboons. Animal Behaviour.

The data are openly available on OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YH2BW). Download the file and save it in your project folder. Please cite the paper and the OSF repository when you use the data.
Download dataset_mothering_behaviors_Anonymized.csv
Each row is one infant in one month: 582 infant-months from 80 infants of 49 mothers. The variables you need:






Variable
Meaning



immature_ID
infant ID


mother_ID
mother ID (some mothers have several infants in the data)


age
infant age in days


imm_focal_duration_sec
focal observation time of the infant in this month (seconds)


normal_approach_received_freq
number of approaches received from the mother




xdata <- read.csv("dataset_mothering_behaviors_Anonymized.csv")


xdata <- xdata[, !duplicated(names(xdata))]          # 'immature_ID' appears twice
xdata$approaches <- xdata$normal_approach_received_freq
xdata$hours      <- xdata$imm_focal_duration_sec / 3600
xdata$age.months <- xdata$age / 30.44
xdata$z.age      <- as.numeric(scale(xdata$age))

title: Exercises · Session 11
text:
Exercise 1: explore the data
How many rows, infants and mothers are there? How many mothers have more than one infant in the data? Plot the rate of approaches (per hour) against age, with one line per infant.






Solution






nrow(xdata)

#> [1] 582

length(unique(xdata$immature_ID))

#> [1] 80

length(unique(xdata$mother_ID))

#> [1] 49

sum(tapply(xdata$immature_ID, xdata$mother_ID, function(x) length(unique(x))) > 1)

#> [1] 19

xdata$rate <- xdata$approaches / xdata$hours
ggplot(xdata, aes(age.months, rate, group = immature_ID)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .3, colour = "#1b6f8a") +
  labs(x = "Age (months)", y = "Approaches per hour")







Each infant contributes several months, and several infants share a mother: the rows are not independent, and the data have two nested grouping factors (infants within mothers).

title: Exercises · Session 11
section: Exercise 2: the model we already know
text:
Exercise 2: the model we already know
Fit a Poisson GLM of approaches with z.age as predictor. Why do you need an offset, and what does it look like? Interpret the age effect, and check for overdispersion.






Solution






glm.mod <- glm(approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)), family = poisson, data = xdata)
summary(glm.mod)$coefficients

#>               Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.1129134 0.04586247 -2.462001 1.381643e-02
#> z.age       -0.2442834 0.04642188 -5.262247 1.423057e-07

exp(coef(glm.mod)["z.age"])                                   # rate ratio per SD of age

#>     z.age 
#> 0.7832656

sum(residuals(glm.mod, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(glm.mod)   # dispersion

#> [1] 1.555269


Observation time differs between rows, so we model the rate of approaches: offset(log(hours)) (see offset). The GLM reports a clear decline of approaches with age. The dispersion ratio is above 1: the counts vary more than a Poisson model expects (overdispersion), often a symptom of ignored structure.

title: Exercises · Session 11
section: Exercise 3: add a random intercept for infants
text:
Exercise 3: add a random intercept for infants
Fit the same model with a random intercept for immature_ID. What happens to the age effect and its standard error?






Solution






ri.mod <- glmer(approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)) + (1 | immature_ID),
                family = poisson, data = xdata,
                control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
summary(ri.mod)$coefficients

#>                Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.35153921 0.10512521 -3.344005 0.0008257829
#> z.age       -0.06841068 0.06551286 -1.044233 0.2963776425

VarCorr(ri.mod)

#>  Groups      Name        Std.Dev.
#>  immature_ID (Intercept) 0.64346


The picture changes completely: the age effect is much smaller and no longer significant. Infants differ strongly in their baseline rate (SD of the random intercept), and because infants are observed at different ages, the GLM mistook differences between infants for a change with age.

title: Exercises · Session 11
text:
Exercise 4: infants within mothers
Several infants share a mother. Add a random intercept for mother_ID. Look at the output: what does the message boundary (singular) fit mean here?






Solution






ri2.mod <- glmer(approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)) + (1 | mother_ID) + (1 | immature_ID),
                 family = poisson, data = xdata,
                 control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
VarCorr(ri2.mod)

#>  Groups      Name        Std.Dev.
#>  immature_ID (Intercept) 0.64344 
#>  mother_ID   (Intercept) 0.00000

isSingular(ri2.mod)

#> [1] TRUE


The SD of the mother intercept is estimated as zero: once infants’ baselines are modelled, there is no additional variation between mothers that the data can detect. This is a singular fit. It is not an error, and the fixed effects are unchanged. Whether to keep the term depends on the design, not on the fit: with a nested design, many researchers keep it to represent the structure of the data.

title: Exercises · Session 11
section: Exercise 5: random slopes, as in the paper
text:
Exercise 5: random slopes, as in the paper
Dal Pesco et al. (2026) included random slopes of age within both mother and infant, without correlations between intercepts and slopes. Fit this model. Which variance components are estimated as (near) zero?






Solution






rs.mod <- glmer(approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)) +
                  (1 + z.age || mother_ID) + (1 + z.age || immature_ID),
                family = poisson, data = xdata,
                control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
VarCorr(rs.mod)

#>  Groups        Name        Std.Dev.
#>  immature_ID   z.age       0.000000
#>  immature_ID.1 (Intercept) 0.638724
#>  mother_ID     z.age       0.076766
#>  mother_ID.1   (Intercept) 0.000000

summary(rs.mod)$coefficients

#>                Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.35100931 0.10487605 -3.346897 0.0008172162
#> z.age       -0.07138771 0.06946104 -1.027737 0.3040733560


Again some components sit at zero (singular fit), but the estimate of the age effect barely changes. Removing the correlations (||) is a common first step when complex structures do not converge (see convergence failure); the paper reports the same reason.

title: Exercises · Session 11
section: Exercise 6: test the age effect and check the model
text:
Exercise 6: test the age effect and check the model
Test the age effect with a likelihood-ratio test, keeping the random-effects structure. Then check the dispersion of the final model.






Solution






rs.null <- glmer(approaches ~ 1 + offset(log(hours)) +
                   (1 + z.age || mother_ID) + (1 + z.age || immature_ID),
                 family = poisson, data = xdata,
                 control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
anova(rs.null, rs.mod)

#> Data: xdata
#> Models:
#> rs.null: approaches ~ 1 + offset(log(hours)) + (1 + z.age || mother_ID) + (1 + z.age || immature_ID)
#> rs.mod: approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)) + (1 + z.age || mother_ID) + (1 + z.age || immature_ID)
#>         npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
#> rs.null    5 1302.4 1324.2 -646.19   1292.4                     
#> rs.mod     6 1303.3 1329.5 -645.66   1291.3 1.0623  1     0.3027

sum(residuals(rs.mod, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(rs.mod)   # dispersion

#> [1] 1.104892


No evidence for a change in maternal approaches with age once the non-independence is modelled. The dispersion ratio is now close to 1: the overdispersion of the GLM was largely due to differences between infants.

title: Exercises · Session 11
text:
Exercise 7: plot the result
Plot the model-predicted rate of approaches over age: one line per infant, plus the population-average line.






Solution






nd <- transform(xdata, hours = 1)                                   # rate per hour
nd$p_inf <- predict(rs.mod, newdata = nd, type = "response")
avg <- data.frame(age.months = seq(0, 18, by = .5), hours = 1)

avg$p <- predict(rs.mod, newdata = avg, type = "response", re.form = NA)  # without random effects

ggplot(nd, aes(age.months, p_inf, group = immature_ID)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .25, colour = "#1b6f8a") +
  geom_line(data = avg, aes(age.months, p), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#c0392b", linewidth = 1.3) +

title: Glossary
text:
Short explanations of terms that come up again and again. Labels show where a term is introduced: LM = Linear Models in R (with session number), ORES = Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science, TAE = Testing for Absence and Equivalence, WS = short workshops.
Entries marked Problem describe something that can go wrong, with steps towards a solution under What to do about it?

title: Glossary
text:
A

AIC (Akaike information criterion)
LM 09
A measure of how well a model predicts new data, balancing fit against the number of parameters. Lower is better. Only differences between models fitted to the same data are meaningful; ΔAIC < 2 means the models are hard to tell apart. See also model selection.


Alpha spending
ORES
In a sequential analysis, the overall type I error rate (α, usually .05) is distributed (“spent”) across the planned interim looks, so that the error rate over all looks stays at α. Common spending functions are Pocock and O’Brien–Fleming.


Assumptions (of the linear model)
LM 02–03
The linear model assumes that (1) observations are independent, (2) the relationship between predictors and response is linear (on the link scale), (3) residuals have constant variance (homoscedasticity) and (4) residuals are normally distributed. Independence matters most, normality least. Check assumptions with residual plots, not with significance tests.

title: Glossary
text:
B

Bayes factor
TAE
The ratio of how well two hypotheses predicted the observed data, e.g. BF01 = 5: the data are five times more likely under H0 than under H1. Unlike a p-value, it can quantify evidence for the null. Depends on the prior for the effect under H1, so report and justify it.

title: Glossary
text:
C

Centring
LM 03, 05
Subtracting a value (usually the mean, or a meaningful reference such as trial 1) from a predictor. It changes the meaning of the intercept and of main effects in models with interactions, but not the fit of the model. See also z-transformation.


Collinearity
LM 03 Problem
Two or more predictors are strongly correlated, so the model cannot separate their effects. Symptoms: large standard errors, estimates that change a lot when a predictor is added or removed. Diagnose with variance inflation factors (car::vif(), performance::check_collinearity()); VIF > 5–10 is often taken as a warning sign.

What to do about it?

Ask whether both predictors are needed for the research question.
Combine them (e.g. into an index or a principal component) if they measure the same thing.
Accept wide intervals: collinearity is a property of the data, not an error. Do not drop predictors just to make p-values smaller.




Complete separation
LM 10 Problem
In a binomial model, a predictor (or combination) perfectly predicts the 0/1 outcome, e.g. all animals in one condition chose “yes”. The maximum-likelihood estimate is then infinite: huge estimates and standard errors, warnings such as “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”.

What to do about it?

Check the cross-tabulation of predictor and response to find the cause.
Use penalised (Firth) logistic regression (logistf, brglm2) or a Bayesian model with a weakly informative prior.
Report the pattern descriptively; it may be the most informative result.




Confidence interval
LM 02
A range computed so that, across many repetitions of the study, 95% of such intervals contain the true value. It does not mean that this particular interval contains the true value with 95% probability; that is the interpretation of a Bayesian credible interval.


Contrasts and dummy coding
LM 04
How a categorical predictor is turned into numbers. Dummy (treatment) coding, R’s default, compares each level with a reference level. Sum coding compares each level with the grand mean, which makes main effects interpretable in models with interactions. Set with contrasts(); check what R did with model.matrix().


Convergence failure
LM 11 Problem
The fitting algorithm did not reliably find the maximum of the likelihood, e.g. lme4’s “Model failed to converge with max|grad| = …”. Common in mixed models with complex random effects, few levels of a grouping factor, or predictors on very different scales. The estimates may or may not be trustworthy.

What to do about it?

z-transform or rescale continuous predictors.
Try another optimizer: control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"), or compare all with allFit(). If they give the same estimates, the warning is usually a false alarm.
Increase the number of iterations, e.g. optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5).
Check for a singular fit; simplify the random-effects structure step by step (e.g. drop the correlations first: (1 + x || id)).
Consider glmmTMB or a Bayesian model (brms), where priors stabilise the fit.




Cook’s distance
LM 02
A measure of how much the model’s estimates change when a single observation is removed. Large values flag influential cases. See influential cases.


Credible interval
WS Bayes, TAE
In Bayesian statistics, an interval that contains the parameter with a given probability (e.g. 95%), given the model, the data and the prior.

title: Glossary
text:
D

Degrees of freedom
LM 02
Roughly, the number of observations minus the number of estimated parameters. They determine the shape of the t- and F-distributions used for tests. In mixed models they are not well defined, which is why lme4 reports no p-values for lmer().


Divergent transitions
WS Bayes Problem
A warning from Stan that the sampler had trouble exploring parts of the posterior. Even a few divergences can bias results.

What to do about it?

Increase adapt_delta (e.g. control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)).
Use more informative priors, especially on standard deviations.
Simplify or reparameterise the model; check for weakly identified parameters.




Dummy coding
See contrasts and dummy coding.

title: Glossary
text:
E

Effect size
LM 02
How large an effect is, in units that matter: a raw difference (e.g. grams, seconds), a standardised difference (Cohen’s d), an odds ratio, or a change in probability. Report it with a confidence interval; a p-value alone says nothing about size.


Equivalence test (TOST)
TAE
Tests whether an effect is smaller than the smallest effect size of interest. Two one-sided tests check whether the effect is significantly above −SESOI and significantly below +SESOI. If both are significant, the effect is “statistically equivalent” to zero.


Estimated marginal means
LM 04
Model-based means for each level of a factor (or combination of factors), averaged over the other predictors. Computed with emmeans; the basis for pairwise comparisons and for reporting results on the response scale.

title: Glossary
text:
F

Failure to converge
See convergence failure.


Fixed effect
LM 11
A model parameter that is the same for all units, e.g. the average effect of age. In mixed models, contrasted with random effects, which vary between units.


Full–null model comparison
LM 09
Comparing the full model (with the predictors of interest) with a null model that lacks them but keeps all control predictors and random effects. A likelihood-ratio test of the two protects against cryptic multiple testing when there are several test predictors.

title: Glossary
text:
H

Heteroscedasticity
LM 02–03 Problem
The residual variance is not constant, e.g. it increases with the fitted values (a “funnel” in the residual plot). Standard errors and p-values can then be wrong.

What to do about it?

Ask whether the response type calls for a GLM (counts and proportions are heteroscedastic by nature).
Transform the response (e.g. log) if this is meaningful.
Model the variance explicitly (glmmTMB with dispformula, nlme::gls), or use robust standard errors (sandwich).

title: Glossary
text:
I

Influential cases
LM 02 Problem
Single observations that strongly change the results (see Cook’s distance), often outliers with unusual predictor values.

What to do about it?

Check for data errors first.
Fit the model with and without these cases and report both if conclusions differ.
Do not delete cases just because they are inconvenient; decide on exclusion rules in advance (see preregistration).




Interaction
LM 05
The effect of one predictor depends on the value of another, e.g. age affects foraging differently in two populations. In R: y ~ a * b. With an interaction in the model, the “main effects” are conditional effects at the zero point of the other predictor, so centring matters.


Intercept
LM 02
The predicted response when all predictors are zero (or at their reference level). Only meaningful if zero is a meaningful value, which is one reason for centring.

title: Glossary
text:
L

Likelihood-ratio test
LM 09–11
Compares two nested models by how much the likelihood improves with the extra parameters. In R: anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq"). The standard way to test effects in GLMs and GLMMs.


Link function
LM 10
In a GLM, the function that connects the linear predictor to the expected response, e.g. the log link for counts (Poisson) and the logit link for probabilities (binomial). Coefficients are on the link scale; transform them back (e.g. exp(), plogis()) or plot predictions to interpret them.


Log-odds (logit)
LM 10
The scale of binomial models: log(p / (1 − p)). 0 corresponds to p = .5; ±2 to about .12 and .88. A coefficient is the change in log-odds per unit of the predictor; exp() turns it into an odds ratio.

title: Glossary
text:
M

Model selection
LM 09
Choosing among candidate models. For confirmatory questions, specify the model in advance and test it (e.g. full–null comparison). For exploratory or predictive questions, compare a small set of plausible models with AIC. Avoid stepwise selection by p-values (see overfitting).

title: Glossary
text:
O

Offset
LM 10
A term in a count model whose coefficient is fixed at 1, used when observation time or effort differs between observations. With a log link, offset(log(hours)) turns a model of counts into a model of rates (counts per hour), without estimating an extra parameter.


Optional stopping
ORES Problem
Testing repeatedly as data come in and stopping as soon as p < .05. This inflates the type I error rate far above 5% (see the simulation on the ORES page).

What to do about it?

Fix the sample size in advance, based on a power analysis.
If you want to look early, plan a sequential analysis with alpha spending.
Bayesian analyses are less affected, but their error rates still depend on the stopping rule; plan it.




Overdispersion
LM 10 Problem
The data vary more than the model assumes. A Poisson model assumes variance = mean; real counts usually vary more. Ignoring it gives too small standard errors and too many false positives. Check with the ratio of residual deviance (or Pearson χ²) to residual df (≫ 1 is a warning sign), performance::check_overdispersion() or DHARMa.

What to do about it?

Check for missing predictors or non-independence first; overdispersion is often a symptom.
Use a negative binomial model (MASS::glm.nb, glmmTMB(family = nbinom2)).
In GLMMs, an observation-level random effect, (1 | obs), can absorb extra variation.
For many zeros, consider zero-inflation.




Overfitting
LM 09 Problem
The model fits noise in the sample rather than the underlying pattern, usually because it has too many parameters for the amount of data. It fits the sample well but predicts new data poorly, and its effects are overestimated.

What to do about it?

Limit the number of predictors (a common rule of thumb: at least 10–20 observations per parameter).
Specify the model from the research question, not from the data.
Evaluate predictions on new data or with cross-validation.

title: Glossary
text:
P

Partial pooling
LM 11
What random effects do: estimates for each individual are pulled towards the overall mean, more strongly for individuals with little data. A compromise between ignoring individuals (complete pooling) and estimating each one separately (no pooling).


Polynomial term
LM 08
A squared (or higher-order) predictor, e.g. y ~ age + I(age^2), to model curved relationships within the linear model. Centre the predictor first to reduce collinearity between the terms, or use poly().


Power
LM 08, WS Power
The probability of detecting an effect of a given size, if it exists. Depends on effect size, sample size, variability and α. For complex models, estimate it by simulation (see power analysis by simulation).


Preregistration
ORES
A time-stamped plan of hypotheses, design, sample size and analysis, written before the data are collected or seen. It separates confirmatory from exploratory analyses. Platforms: OSF, AsPredicted.


Prior, posterior
WS Bayes, TAE
In Bayesian statistics, the prior expresses what is plausible about a parameter before seeing the data; the posterior combines prior and data (via the likelihood). Check what your priors imply with a prior predictive check.


Pseudoreplication
LM 11 Problem
Treating repeated observations of the same unit (animal, group, session) as independent. The effective sample size is overstated, so standard errors are too small and false positives too frequent.

What to do about it?

Identify the unit of observation and all grouping factors before the analysis.
Include random effects for them, with random slopes for predictors that vary within units.
Alternatively, aggregate to one value per unit (loses information but is valid).




p-value
LM 02
The probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one, if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and p > .05 is not evidence for “no effect” (see equivalence test).

title: Glossary
text:
R

Random effects (random intercepts and slopes)
LM 11
Parameters that vary between units of a grouping factor (e.g. chimps), modelled as coming from a common distribution. A random intercept, (1 | id), lets units differ in their baseline; a random slope, (1 + x | id), lets the effect of x differ between units. Random slopes are needed for predictors that vary within units, otherwise tests of these predictors are too liberal.


Reference level
LM 04
With dummy coding, the factor level that the intercept refers to and that all other levels are compared with. R uses the first level alphabetically; change it with relevel() or factor(..., levels = ).


Registered report
ORES
A publication format in which the introduction, methods and analysis plan are peer-reviewed before data collection. If accepted in principle, the paper is published regardless of the results.


Residuals
LM 02
Observed minus predicted values. Plots of residuals against fitted values and predictors are the main tool for checking assumptions. For GLMs and GLMMs, use simulated (quantile) residuals from DHARMa.


Rhat and effective sample size (ESS)
WS Bayes
Convergence diagnostics in Bayesian models. Rhat compares chains; values above 1.01 suggest they have not converged. ESS is the number of effectively independent draws; it should be at least a few hundred per parameter.


ROPE (region of practical equivalence)
TAE
A range of parameter values considered practically equivalent to zero (defined via the SESOI). If (almost) the whole posterior lies inside the ROPE, the effect is accepted as practically zero.


3Rs
ORES
Principles for the ethical use of animals in research: Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. Good statistical planning (power analysis, sequential designs) contributes directly to Reduction.

title: Glossary
text:
S

Sequential analysis
ORES
A design with planned interim analyses, at which data collection can stop for efficacy or futility, while alpha spending keeps the overall error rate at α. With animals, it reduces the expected number of animals needed. In R: rpact.


SESOI (smallest effect size of interest)
TAE
The smallest effect that would be theoretically or practically meaningful. Needed for equivalence tests, ROPEs and power analyses. Justify it from theory, previous studies or practical considerations, and preregister it.


Singular fit
LM 11 Problem
lme4’s message “boundary (singular) fit”: a random-effect variance is estimated as (nearly) zero or a correlation as ±1. The random-effects structure is too complex for the data, often because a grouping factor has few levels.

What to do about it?

Inspect VarCorr(model) to see which component is at the boundary.
Simplify: first remove the random-effect correlations (||), then random slopes with (near-)zero variance, guided by the design rather than by p-values.
Keep in mind that removing random slopes for within-unit predictors makes tests of these predictors too liberal; report what you did.
A Bayesian model (brms) with weakly informative priors avoids estimates at the boundary.




Standard error
LM 02
The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples: how much the estimate would vary if the study were repeated. The basis of confidence intervals and tests.


Stopping for futility
ORES
Ending a study early at a planned interim analysis because the effect is unlikely to reach significance even with the full sample. Saves resources and, in animal research, animals.

title: Glossary
text:
Z

z-transformation (standardisation)
LM 03
Subtracting the mean of a predictor and dividing by its standard deviation: scale(x). The predictor then has mean 0 and SD 1, so coefficients are the effect of a one-SD change. Makes effects of predictors on different scales comparable and often helps models to converge.


Zero-inflation
LM 10, WS GLMMs Problem
More zeros than a Poisson or negative binomial model predicts, e.g. because some animals never show a behaviour. Ignoring it can bias estimates. Check with DHARMa::testZeroInflation() or performance::check_zeroinflation().

What to do about it?

Ask where the extra zeros come from (e.g. animals that were never in a position to show the behaviour).
Fit a zero-inflated or hurdle model with glmmTMB (ziformula = ~ 1); see advanced GLMMs.
Sometimes a negative binomial model alone already accounts for the zeros; compare the models.

title: 11 · Generalized linear mixed models (GLMM)
section: Simulate first: do chimpanzees understand mechanisms?
text:
Simulate first: do chimpanzees understand mechanisms?
Chimpanzees choose into which of two boxes a grape is dropped. The Safe box clearly guarantees delivery; in the Risky box, the grape seems to get stuck. In fact, both boxes always deliver.


RQ1: Do chimps prefer the Safe box on trial 1?

RQ2: Does this preference change over trials?


Ongoing study with the MPI EVA, Leipzig; preregistered. The data do not exist yet: these are simulated data of what we expect, so we know the true answer: a clear Safe preference on trial 1 (70%), no average change over trials, but chimps that differ in whether they drift towards Safe or Risky.


Simulation codeTRUE.INT   <- qlogis(0.70)  # log-odds of choosing Safe on trial 1 (Side = left)
TRUE.TRIAL <- 0             # average change per trial (log-odds)
TRUE.SIDE  <- 0.3           # small bias towards the right side
SD.INT     <- 0.8           # between-chimp SD of the intercept
SD.SLOPE   <- 0.05          # between-chimp SD of the trial slope (per trial)

side_sequence <- function() {           # 5 x right, 5 x left; max. 2 in a row
  repeat {
    s <- sample(rep(0:1, 5))
    if (max(rle(s)$lengths) <= 2) return(s)
  }
}

sim_chimps <- function(n = 15, b0 = TRUE.INT, b.trial = TRUE.TRIAL, b.side = TRUE.SIDE,
                       sd.int = SD.INT, sd.slope = SD.SLOPE) {
  ids <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:n)
  u0 <- setNames(rnorm(n, 0, sd.int), ids); u1 <- setNames(rnorm(n, 0, sd.slope), ids)
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ids, function(id)
    data.frame(subject = id, session = rep(1:4, each = 10), trial = 1:40,
               side_safe = unlist(replicate(4, side_sequence(), simplify = FALSE)))))
  d$trial_c <- d$trial - 1                       # first-trial centred (as preregistered)
  eta <- b0 + u0[d$subject] + (b.trial + u1[d$subject]) * d$trial_c + b.side * d$side_safe
  d$safe <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(eta))
  d
}

set.seed(120)
xdata <- sim_chimps()      # 15 chimps x 4 sessions x 10 trials


600 choices, but only 15 chimpanzees

Codeps  <- aggregate(safe ~ subject + session, xdata, mean)
chg <- tapply(ps$safe, ps$subject, function(x) x[4] - x[1])
ord <- names(sort(chg))                                   # strongest drift to Risky first
gd  <- xdata
gd$subject <- factor(gd$subject, levels = rev(ord))
gd$choice  <- factor(ifelse(gd$safe == 1, "Safe", "Risky"), levels = c("Safe", "Risky"))
gd$session <- factor(paste("session", gd$session))

ggplot(gd, aes(trial, subject, fill = choice)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(~ session, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Safe = col_safe, Risky = col_risk), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 10, 20, 30, 40), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Trial", y = "Chimpanzee", subtitle = "All 600 choices, one row per chimpanzee") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.3, "lines"), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8))







Chimps differ in their overall preference and in how their preference changes. Choices of the same chimp are more similar to each other than to choices of other chimps: they are not independent. A GLM treats the 600 choices as 600 pieces of information (pseudoreplication).
Three models

glm.mod <- glm(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe, family = binomial, data = xdata)

# random intercepts
ri.mod  <- glmer(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 | subject),
                 family = binomial, data = xdata,
                 control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# random intercepts + random slopes
rs.mod  <- glmer(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 + trial_c | subject),
                 family = binomial, data = xdata,
                 control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))


Codend <- expand.grid(trial_c = 0:39, subject = unique(xdata$subject), side_safe = 0.5)
nd$trial <- nd$trial_c + 1
labs3 <- c("GLM", "GLMM (1 | subject)", "GLMM (1 + trial_c | subject)")
ln <- rbind(transform(nd, p = predict(glm.mod, newdata = nd, type = "response"), model = labs3[1]),
            transform(nd, p = predict(ri.mod,  newdata = nd, type = "response"), model = labs3[2]),
            transform(nd, p = predict(rs.mod,  newdata = nd, type = "response"), model = labs3[3]))
ln$model <- factor(ln$model, levels = labs3)

ggplot(ln, aes(trial, p, group = subject, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(alpha = .7, linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_glm, col_ri, col_glmm), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Trial", y = "Predicted P(Safe)", caption = "Lines = model-predicted probabilities per chimp")







What changes? And what is true?

Codecg <- summary(glm.mod)$coefficients; cri <- summary(ri.mod)$coefficients; crs <- summary(rs.mod)$coefficients
rq <- c("RQ1: Safe preference on trial 1\n(intercept, log-odds)", "RQ2: change per 10 trials\n(log-odds)")
cmp <- data.frame(
  term  = factor(rep(rq, each = 3), levels = rq),
  model = factor(rep(labs3, 2), levels = rev(labs3)),
  est = c(cg["(Intercept)", 1], cri["(Intercept)", 1], crs["(Intercept)", 1],
          10 * c(cg["trial_c", 1], cri["trial_c", 1], crs["trial_c", 1])),
  se  = c(cg["(Intercept)", 2], cri["(Intercept)", 2], crs["(Intercept)", 2],
          10 * c(cg["trial_c", 2], cri["trial_c", 2], crs["trial_c", 2])))
truth <- data.frame(term = factor(rq, levels = rq), val = c(TRUE.INT, 10 * TRUE.TRIAL))

ggplot(cmp, aes(est, model, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(data = truth, aes(xintercept = val), colour = col_true, linetype = "longdash") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = est - 1.96 * se, xmax = est + 1.96 * se), height = .15, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("GLM" = col_glm, "GLMM (1 | subject)" = col_ri,
                                 "GLMM (1 + trial_c | subject)" = col_glmm), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Estimate with 95% CI (dashed line = true value)", y = NULL)










RQ1: intercept
RQ2: trial



GLM
1.08 (p < .001)
-0.022 (p = .004)


GLMM: intercepts
1.50 (p < .001)
-0.031 (p < .001)


GLMM: + slopes
1.15 (p < .001)
-0.013 (p = .507)



All models find the Safe preference on trial 1. But the GLM and the random-intercept model report a “significant” decline over trials, which does not exist. Only the model with random slopes gets RQ2 right.
Was this just bad luck? 1000 simulations

# Repeat the whole study 1000 times and record the p-value of the trial effect
# (fit_chimps() is defined in the R script; takes a few minutes)
set.seed(2026)
sims <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(1000, suppressMessages(fit_chimps(sim_chimps())))))


Codesims <- read.csv("../../data/sim_results_chimps_1000.csv")
fp   <- colMeans(sims < 0.05)
sv <- data.frame(model = factor(labs3, levels = labs3), val = as.numeric(fp[c("glm.p", "ri.p", "rs.p")]))

ggplot(sv, aes(model, val, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = .6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, linetype = "longdash", colour = col_true) +
  annotate("text", x = .55, y = .075, label = "nominal 5%", hjust = 0, colour = col_true) +
  geom_text(aes(label = pc(val)), vjust = -.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_glm, col_ri, col_glmm), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, .5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Significant trial effect", subtitle = "1000 simulations; true average change = 0")







With a true average change of zero, the GLM finds a “significant” change in 32% of the runs, the random-intercept model in 37%, and the model with random slopes in 9%, much closer to the nominal 5%. The small remaining excess comes from the Wald tests that glmer() reports by default, which are slightly too liberal with only 15 individuals; likelihood-ratio tests or a parametric bootstrap do better.

Simulating your expected data lets you check your planned model before you collect a single data point.

title: Advanced GLMMs with glmmTMB
text:
glmmTMB is an R package for fitting generalized linear mixed models by maximum likelihood, like lme4::glmer() from session 11. Its strength is flexibility: it handles many distributions and model parts that glmer() cannot, and it is usually fast and stable.
It is the natural next step when the data do not fit a Poisson or binomial GLMM, which is common with behavioural data, for example counts of rare behaviours with many zeros.

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
text:
Four tests, one dataset
Classical significance tests can do much more than reject an effect of exactly zero. Lakens (2022, ch. 9) distinguishes four kinds of tests. They differ only in which hypothesis is tested, so all four can be applied to the same data: each answers a different question.

The data
Participants solve a puzzle; we measure the solution time in seconds. A control group is compared with a training group (500 participants each). The effect of interest is the time saved by training, Δ = control − training.

The smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) is 2 seconds: savings below 2 s are too small to matter in practice.
A theory predicts savings between 0.5 and 2.5 s.


set.seed(4)
control  <- rnorm(500, mean = 20,   sd = 5)
training <- rnorm(500, mean = 18.8, sd = 5)

sesoi <- 2                     # smallest effect size of interest (s)
lower <- 0.5; upper <- 2.5     # range predicted by the theory (s)

The observed saving is Δ = 1.25 s, 95% CI [0.65, 1.85], 90% CI [0.75, 1.76].


The four tests at a glance


Code
lim <- c(-4, 4)
panels <- c("A: two-sided null hypothesis test", "B: interval hypothesis test",
            "C: equivalence test", "D: minimum effect test")
reg <- function(panel, xmin, xmax, hyp) data.frame(panel, xmin, xmax, hyp)
regions <- rbind(
  reg(panels[1], lim[1], lim[2], "H1"),
  reg(panels[2], c(lim[1], upper), c(lower, lim[2]), "H0"), reg(panels[2], lower, upper, "H1"),
  reg(panels[3], c(lim[1], sesoi), c(-sesoi, lim[2]), "H1"), reg(panels[3], -sesoi, sesoi, "H0"),
  reg(panels[4], c(lim[1], sesoi), c(-sesoi, lim[2]), "H1"), reg(panels[4], -sesoi, sesoi, "H0"))
regions$hyp[regions$panel == panels[3]] <- ifelse(regions$hyp[regions$panel == panels[3]] == "H0", "H1", "H0")
regions$panel <- factor(regions$panel, levels = panels)
nil <- data.frame(panel = factor(panels[1], levels = panels), x = 0)
ci  <- data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels), est = est,
                  lo = c(t95$conf.int[1], rep(t90$conf.int[1], 3)),
                  hi = c(t95$conf.int[2], rep(t90$conf.int[2], 3)))

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = regions, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -.4, ymax = .4, fill = hyp), alpha = .35) +
  geom_segment(data = nil, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = -.4, yend = .4), colour = col_h0, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(data = ci, aes(y = 0, xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = .25, linewidth = 1, colour = col_navy) +
  geom_point(data = ci, aes(est, 0), size = 2.6, colour = col_navy) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, strip.position = "left", dir = "v") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(H0 = col_h0, H1 = col_h1), name = NULL,
                    labels = c(H0 = "null hypothesis (H0)", H1 = "alternative hypothesis (H1)")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-sesoi, 0, lower, sesoi, upper), labels = c("-2", "0", "0.5", "2", "2.5"),
                     limits = lim, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Time saved by training, ", Delta, " (s)")), y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top")








Figure 1: Two-sided null hypothesis test (A), interval hypothesis test (B), equivalence test (C) and minimum effect test (D). Red: values in the null hypothesis; blue: values in the alternative hypothesis. Point and bar: our estimate with 95% CI (A) or 90% CI (B–D). Adapted from Lakens (2022), Fig. 9.1; this figure is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.







A: two-sided null hypothesis test
Question: Is there any effect at all? H0: Δ = 0. H1: Δ ≠ 0. The classic t-test; significant if the 95% CI excludes 0.

t.test(control, training, var.equal = TRUE)

#> 
#>  Two Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  control and training
#> t = 4.0852, df = 998, p-value = 4.757e-05
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.6510149 1.8545975
#> sample estimates:
#> mean of x mean of y 
#>  19.85426  18.60146


Result: p < .001. Training saves time, but this test says nothing about whether the saving is large enough to matter.


B: interval hypothesis test
Question: Does the effect fall within the range the theory predicts? H0: Δ ≤ 0.5 or Δ ≥ 2.5. H1: 0.5 < Δ < 2.5. Two one-sided tests, one against each bound; the prediction is supported if both are significant, i.e. the 90% CI lies inside the predicted range.

# H0a: Delta <= 0.5 (test: greater than the lower bound)
p_lo <- t.test(control, training, mu = lower,
               alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
# H0b: Delta >= 2.5 (test: less than the upper bound)
p_hi <- t.test(control, training, mu = upper,
               alternative = "less", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
c(p_lower = p_lo, p_upper = p_hi, p = max(p_lo, p_hi))

#>      p_lower      p_upper            p 
#> 7.133457e-03 2.569832e-05 7.133457e-03


Result: p = .007. The saving lies within the predicted range of 0.5 to 2.5 s.


C: equivalence test (TOST)
Question: Is the effect too small to matter? H0: Δ ≤ −2 or Δ ≥ 2. H1: −2 < Δ < 2. The same two one-sided tests as in B, now against −SESOI and +SESOI; equivalence is shown if the 90% CI lies inside the equivalence bounds.

# H0a: Delta <= -2 (test: greater than the lower equivalence bound)
p_lo <- t.test(control, training, mu = -sesoi,
               alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
# H0b: Delta >= 2 (test: less than the upper equivalence bound)
p_hi <- t.test(control, training, mu = sesoi,
               alternative = "less", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
c(p_lower = p_lo, p_upper = p_hi, p = max(p_lo, p_hi))

#>      p_lower      p_upper            p 
#> 2.791839e-25 7.502522e-03 7.502522e-03


Result: p = .008. The saving is statistically equivalent to zero within ±2 s: it is real (test A), but smaller than anything we consider meaningful.


D: minimum effect test
Question: Is the effect larger than the smallest effect of interest? H0: −2 ≤ Δ ≤ 2. H1: Δ < −2 or Δ > 2. The reverse of the equivalence test; here we test only the direction the theory predicts (Δ > 2).

# H0: Delta <= 2 (test: greater than the SESOI)
t.test(control, training, mu = sesoi,
       alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value

#> [1] 0.9924975


Result: p = .992. We cannot claim a saving larger than 2 s.


With the TOSTER package
The R package TOSTER runs tests C and D in one call and adds effect sizes and plots:

library(TOSTER)
# C: equivalence test
t_TOST(x = control, y = training, eqb = sesoi, var.equal = TRUE)
# D: minimum effect test
t_TOST(x = control, y = training, eqb = sesoi, var.equal = TRUE, hypothesis = "MET")



Summary









Test
Question
H0
Result here




A: two-sided null hypothesis test
Any effect?
Δ = 0
rejected: training saves time


B: interval hypothesis test
Within the predicted range?
Δ ≤ 0.5 or Δ ≥ 2.5
rejected: prediction supported


C: equivalence test
Too small to matter?
|Δ| ≥ 2
rejected: equivalent to zero


D: minimum effect test
Larger than the SESOI?
|Δ| ≤ 2
not rejected



The same data give four different answers because the tests ask four different questions. Which test is appropriate follows from the hypothesis, and should be decided, and preregistered, before the data are seen.

Note: With 500 participants per group, even a saving of about 1 s is detected (A) and shown to be negligible (C). With small samples, typical for animal studies, all four tests are often inconclusive. Planning the sample size for the test you intend to run is part of the course.

Reference: Lakens, D. (2022). Improving your statistical inferences (ch. 9: Equivalence testing and interval hypotheses). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6409077. Licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
